CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
191.0 Car Inspection
1.1 Car Inspection Requirements
At each location where a freight car is placed in a train and mechanical forces are not on duty for the 
purpose of inspecting freight cars, the freight car shall, as a minimum, be inspected for the following 
conditions:
•
Car body:
o
Leaning.
o
Sagging downward.
o
Improperlypositioned truck.
o
Objectdragging below.
o
Objectextending from side.
o
Door insecurely attached.
o
Broken or missing safety appliance.
•
Ladingleaking from a placarded hazardous material car.
•
Insecurecoupling device.
•
Overheated wheel or journal.
•
Broken or cracked wheel.
•
Brake that fails to release.
•
Any other apparent safety hazard likely to cause an accident or casualty before the train arrives 
at its destination.
Thisinspection must be performed on each side of all cars.2.0 Freight Car End, Platform, and Wheel Identification
2.1 Car End Identification
Identify car ends as follows:
•
On cars with one hand brake, the “B” end of the car is the end with the hand brake and the other 
end is the “A” end.
•
On cars with more than one hand brake, the letters “A” and “B” are stenciled on the appropriate 
ends of the car.2.2 Wheel Identification
Car wheel numbers are identified as follows:
•
Axles are designated from the “B” end of the car with number 1 being the axle closest to the “B” 
end.
•
Wheels and journals are designated as either left or right as viewed from the “B” end.
•
Specific wheels are identified using both the axle and wheel designation.

Ax les are designated from the “B ” end of the car with the number 1 ax le closest to the

Wheels and j ournals are designated as either left or right as v iewed from the “B ” end.

The remainder of the platforms are identified as “C ” through “E” beginning at the platform 
immediately adj acent to the “B ” end.

213.0 Coupler Identification
3.1 Coupler Assembly Types
There are three main types of coupler assemblies used in North America. Each coupler head and knuckle 
is marked with a letter indicating its type, E, F, or H. Knuckles are not interchangeable.3.2 Assembly type descriptions
•
Type E – Most common assembly used on all types of freight cars.
•
Type F – Interlocking coupler assembly used on most intermodal and some bulk commodity 
equipment.
•
Type H – “Tight Lock” coupler assembly used on passenger equipment and some work 
equipment.

4.0 Retaining Valves
4.1 Retaining Valve Location
Theretaining valve controls brake cylinder pressure exhaust on a freight car. All freight cars have 
retaining valves located at the “B ” end of the car or on the side near the control valve.4.2 Th ree-Position Retaining Valve
The three-position retaining valve consists of the following positions:
•
Exhaust (E X ) –
Allowsunrestricted passage of brake cylinder pressure to exhaust to atmosphere;
Handle is turned down.
•
High Pressure (H P) –
Restrict the exhaust of brake cylinder pressure at a controlled rate and 
retains 20 pounds of brake cylinder pressure; Handle is 45 degrees below horiz ontal.
•
Slow Direct (S D ): Restrict the exhaust of brake cylinder pressure at a controlled rate to provide a 
blow down time of approximately 86 s

CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
511.0 General Requirements
Crew members are responsible for securing unattended equipment with hand brakes. Equipment is 
considered unattended when left in a manner that the brake system of the equipment cannot be readily 
controlled by a qualified person. Employees must not engage in any unrelated tasks while attending 
equipment.2.0 Hand Brakes
Fully apply hand brakes until the slack is out of the chain and the brake shoes are in contact with the 
wheel. In winter conditions, ensure that braking surfaces are free of ice and snow.
Unlesstesting for securement, hand brakes must be fully released before moving equipment.3.0 Testing Hand Brake Effectiveness
To ensure a sufficient number of hand brakes are applied, release all air brakes and allow sufficient time 
for release. Cause or allow the slack to adjust to verify that the number of hand brakes applied are 
sufficient to prevent equipment from moving. This test must be completed before uncoupling or leaving 
equipment unattended.
When unable to test hand brake effectiveness, apply hand brakes as follows:
•
On grades from 0 to 0.99%, apply hand brakes to at least 20 percent of cars.
•
On grades from 1.0 to 1.29%, apply hand brakes to at least 30 percent of cars.
•
On grades from 1.3 to 1.79%, apply hand brakes to at least 50 percent of cars.
•
On grades 1.8% or higher, apply hand brakes to at least 65 percent of cars.
•
Locomotive hand brakes must not be included in the total hand brake count. If in doubt 
or uncertainty exists as to the number of hand brakes to apply, contact management for 
instructions.4.0 Securing Equipment Following an Emergency Brake Application 
or Train Braking Issue on Heavy or Mountain Grade
When a train experiences an emergency brake application or train braking issue on heavy or mountain 
grade, the following will apply:
•
Immediately secure equipment with hand brakes prior to attempting to recharge the air brake 
system.
•
At minimum, apply hand brakes in accordance with the following:
o
On grades from 1.0 to 1.29%, apply hand brakes to at least 30 percent of cars.
o
On grades from 1.3 to 1.79%, apply hand brakes to at least 50 percent of cars.
o
On grades 1.8% or higher, apply hand brakes to at least 65 percent of cars.
•
Once the air brake system is fully recharged, prior to the release of hand brakes, make an 
automatic brake application sufficient to hold the train.

CPK C | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
5.0 Leaving E q u ip m
ent Unattended
5.1 General Req u irem
ents
Whenleaving railway equipment unattended, the following will apply:
•
Asingle piece of equipment must be left with the hand brake applied.
•
Asingle piece of equipment with a defective hand brake must be left coupled to equipment with 
an operative hand brake.
•
Two or more pieces of equipment must be left with a sufficient number of hand brakes.
•
When hand brakes are not adequate, block the wheels.
•
When it is required to remove equipment from a previously secured track or train, ensure the 
equipment left standing is properly secured with hand brakes.
•
D o not uncouple from or allow equipment to move under its own momentum into standing 
equipment unless it is known that the number of hand brakes applied on the standing equipment 
are sufficient to prevent movement of all equipment.5.2 Leaving Lo c o m
o tive( s ) Unattended
To secure unattended locomotive(s), perform the following:
•
Apply hand brakes to each locomotive.
•
Test hand brake effectiveness.
•
Condition one control stand as a lead locomotive.
o
Independent brake cut in and fully applied.
o
Automatic brake cut in and 20-psi reduction.
o
Generator Field Off.
o
Engine Run and Control / Fuel Pump On.
o
Engine Control Switch to Isolate.
o
Reverser handle removed.
•
Turn off all unnecessary lights and close all windows.
•
Lock all doors on each locomotive, unless being left in one of the following yards or terminals with 
24 hour per day oversight:
o
Artesia, Beaumont, Bensenville, Heavener, Jackson, Kansas City, Kendleton, Laredo, Mason 
City, Meridian, Monroe, Mossville, Nahant, Pittsburg, Saratoga Springs, Shreveport, St. 
Louis, St. Paul, or Wylie.5.3 Leaving a P o rtio n o f a Train o r Cars Unattended
To secure a portion of a train or cars being left unattended, perform the following:
•
Apply a sufficient number of hand brakes.
•
Test hand brake effectiveness.
•
Make an automatic brake reduction sufficient to prevent movement.
•
The locomotive engineer must advise the crewmember when the angle cock can be closed.
•
Cut away from the equipment and ensure an emergency brake application occurs.
•
Leave the angle cock fully open.
o
The angle cock may be closed for the purpose of immediately running around equipment to 
open an angle cock or couple to the other end.

•
Crew members are responsible to verbally confirm that equipment is being left in accordance with 
these instructions.5.4 Leaving a Train Unattended
To secure an unattended train, perform the following:
•
Apply a sufficient number of hand brakes to the car(s) in the train.
•
Test hand brake effectiveness.
•
Apply hand brakes to each locomotive in the lead consist.
•
Leave the lead locomotive of the unattended train conditioned as follows:
o
Independent brake cut in and fully applied.
o
Automatic brake cut in and 20-psi reduction.
o
Generator Field Off.
o
Engine Run and Control / Fuel Pump On.
o
Engine Control Switch to Isolate.
o
Reverser handle removed.
•
Turn off all unnecessary lights and close all windows.
•
Lock all doors on each locomotive, including remotes.

CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
731.0 General Requirements
Employees must use the most efficient means available to maximize fuel efficiency. Thefollowing will 
apply:
•
Locomotive engineers must use the most fuel-efficient methods when operating locomotives, 
consistent with good train handling.
•
Dynamic brake is the preferred method of braking.
•
Whenever possible, avoid increasing the throttle while the automatic brake is applied.
•
Unlessauthorized by timetable or special instruction, power braking above notch 4 is prohibited.
•
When it is known that a train will be delayed, train speed must be reduced to minimize delay time.
•
Avoid unnecessary increases in speed over short distances.2.0 Compliance with Train Document Messages and Other 
Instructions
The locomotive engineer and conductor are jointly responsible to ensure that the number of operating 
locomotives on a train are compliant with train document messages or other related instructions. 
Locomotive engineers must isolate excess locomotive(s) and document locomotive status on the Crew 
Information Form.3.0 Energy Management Systems
When available, use of energy management software is mandatory. Locomotive engineers who have not 
received training are prohibited from operating energy management software.
Issues with energy management systems must be reported to the applicable support desk and reported 
on the required form.4.0 Automatic Engine Start Stop (AESS)
4.1 General
Locomotivesequipped with automatic engine start/stop systems are identified by labels and instructions 
affixed inside the locomotive cab and at the engine start/stop station. Agreen Enabled light will be visible 
on the engine control panel, or the control stand on certain automatic start/stop systems to convey 
system status. Warning horns or bells sound before an automatic shut down or restart occurs. Auto 
start/stop equipped locomotives will automatically shut down when conditions permit. The reverser must 
be centered for AESS to work on trailing locomotives.4.2 Restarting Locomotives Prior to Starting a Movement
Locomotivesequipped with automatic engine start and stop systems may have shut down if the 
locomotive(s) have been inactive for an extended duration of time. If it is suspected that any operative 
locomotive(s) has shut down, or if engine run status is unknown, move the reverser handle in the 
direction of travel to activate the engine start sequence. Wait at least two minutes before starting the train.
CPKC | U n i t e d S t a t e s A i r B r a ke
 a n d T r a i n H a n d l i n g
73

74
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
5.0 Locomotiv e Anti- id ling Req uirements
Locomotives not eq uipped with AESS system must be manually shut down if it is known that the 
locomotive( s) will be idling for more than 15 minutes, and the ambient temperature is expected 
to remain at or above 40 degrees Fahrenheit. I n the case of uncertainty, contact Mechanical. The manual 
shut down req uirement does not apply if the engine must be kept running to:
•
Maintain air pressure for the braking system.
•
Maintain battery charge on the locomotive for the starting systems.
•
Heat or cool the cab or passenger eq uipment for the reasons of health and safety.
•
Perform diagnostic testing and necessary maintenance.
•
Respond to an emergency situation.
CPKC | U n i t e d S t a t e s A i r B r a ke
 a n d T r a i n H a n d l i n g
74

CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
756.0 Pacing 
When it is known that a train will be delayed, the train speed must be reduced to limit delay time and 
amount of fuel consumed. This includes following a slower train, anticipated train meets, and 
maintenance work windows.
The train dispatcher may issue instructions for train speed to be reduced to less than maximum 
authorized timetable speed. To take advantage of areas with descending grade, this restriction only 
applies when the train is operating in throttle. 
When train pacing for an unusually long period of time, take additional locomotives off-line to compensate 
for reduced horsepower needs at lower speeds.

C PK C | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
1.0 HOT- EOT System Setu p
1.1 Installation
•
Thecalibration date shown on the EOT device must not be expired. 
•
Install the EOT
•
From the EOT display, verify that the EOT battery voltage is 12.2 Vor higher.
•
Enter the EOT number in the HOT on the lead locomotive.
•
Press the HOT COMM TEST button and verify on the HOT display that the Comm Testpassed.
•
Aftercharging the train, validate that the pressure displayed on the HOT is within + /- 3 psi of the 
EOT pressure.1.2 Repeating
•
On trains equipped with a mid-train train distributed power locomotive, configure the HOT 
repeater as follows: 
o
DPS Device –
Ensure the HOT is disarmed and the EOT ID is set to z ero.
o
Integrated LX A –
Enter the EOT ID into the HOT. 
o
Quantum Q 3442 –
Enter the EOT ID and place the toggle switch in the repeater position.2.0 Arming the HOT
To arm the HOT:
•
Press the button on the EOT.
•
When the Arming message appears on the HOT, immediately press the Arm button on the HOT.
•
Verify that the HOT indicates Armed or Emergency Enabled.
•
If the system fails to Arm, press the HOT C OMM TEST button to determine communication status 
and repeat the steps above.3.0 Testing the HOT and EOT System
An HOT/EOT system must be tested at the initial terminal or other point of installation to determine that 
the device can initiate an emergency brake application. To test the system, perform the following:
•
Close the angle cock ahead of the last car.
•
Activate the EOT emergency toggle switch in the locomotive cab. 
•
Verify that the cars behind the angle cock go into emergency.
•
Allow 15 seconds for the EOT emergency valve to close before opening the angle cock.
•
Open the angle cock. 
Alternativetesting methods:
•
Test the system with the EOT mounted on the locomotive. Perform a comm test after installation 
on train.
•
Individual components are bench tested by Mechanical. Perform a comm test after installation on 
train.
CPKC | U n i t e d S t a t e s A i r B r a ke
 a n d T r a i n H a n d l i n g
102

CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
1034.0 Disarming the HOT
To disarm the HOT:
•
Initiate the Disarmfunction on the HOT and set the EOT ID code to “00000”.
•
Verify the HOT displays “disarmed” or “emergency disabled” and an EOT ID of 00000.
Disarm the HOT when:
•
Atrain reaches its final terminal.
•
Replacing an HOT or EOT enroute.5.0 Emergency Toggle Switch
The HOT/EOT system must be properly armed to activate an emergency brake application. To initiate an 
EOT emergency brake activation: 
•
Lift the red cover and toggle of the EOT emergency switch.
•
Verify the rear brake pipe pressure reduces to 0 psi.
When an EOT emergency brake activation is initiated, the HOT will continually transmit a series of 
emergency brake commands to the EOT for two minutes or until the EOT acknowledges the command. 
If, after two minutes, the EOT has not responded and the rear brake pipe pressure is not 0 PSI, the 
locomotive engineer will be required to reinitiate the EOT emergency brake activation.6.0 Emergency Application Capability from Rear of Train
All trains must have the ability to initiate an emergency brake application from the rear of the train, except:
•
Locomotivesoperating without cars.
•
Passenger trains.
•
Locals, road switchers, work trains, and yard assignments provided:
o
Train weight does not exceed 4,000 trailing tons.
o
Movement does not operate over heavy or mountain grade or travel a distance farther than 
can normally be operated by a single crew in a single tour of duty.
•
Trains that operate at speeds less than 30 mph and do not operate over heavy or 
mountain grades.7.0 Acceptable Methods for Initiating Emergency Application at 
Rear of Train
Thefollowing methods will fulfil the requirement to initiate an emergency application from the rear of the 
train:
•
An operable HOT and EOT which has been armed and tested at the point of installation.
•
A Distributed Power locomotive at the rear of the train which is linked to the lead locomotive.
•
Helper locomotive(s), caboose, or passenger equipment at the rear of the train provided it is 
equipped with:
o
An emergency brake valve.
o
An employee with a two-way voice radio in communication with the locomotive engineer in 
the lead locomotive.

CPK C | United States Air Brak e and Train Handling

1.0 TrAM Areas
Train Area Marshalling areas are:
•
Defined by a combination of grade and curvature.
•
Divided into six areas.
•
Identified in the subdivision page of the timetable.2.0 Trai n Ty p es
All trains are classified as one of the following:
•
Heavy Bulk :
o
Contains only conventional cars.
o
All cars on the train weigh at least 100 tons and measure 65 feet or less in length.
•
Light Bulk :
o
Contains only conventional cars.
o
All cars on the train weight less than 50 tons and measure 65 feet or less in length.
•
Heavy Uniform:
o
Contains either conventional or multi-platform cars.
o
All cars on the train:

Weigh at least 50 tons per car or platform.

The maximum weight difference between cars or platforms does not exceed 20 tons.

Maximum length difference between cars or platforms is ten feet.
•
Mixed:
o
Any train that does not qualify as one of the train types listed above.4.0 Trai n C o n f i gu rat i o n s
4.1 C o n v en t i o n al Trai n
•
Aconventional train is a train in which all operating locomotives are located at the head end of a 
train.
•
Conventional trains that meet the definition of Heavy Bulk , Light Bulk , or Heavy Uniform must not 
exceed 10,000 feet. Mixed conventional trains must not exceed 10,000 feet or 10,000 tons.
o
Exception: Unless otherwise specified, trains with solid intermodal equipment may operate to 
a maximum length of 12,000 feet.4.2 D i st ri b u t ed P o w er Trai n
•
Adistributed power train is a train in which all operating locomotives are located at the head end 
of the train and in up to three additional positions throughout the train. All locomotives are 
controlled from the head end locomotive consist.
•
The maximum length of a distributed power train must not exceed 14,000 feet.

1095.0 TrAM Messages
TrAM messages contain the following parts:
•
Part 1 – Train Information: provides essential information about the train, including 
train type.
•
Part 2 – Caution Messages: Provides warnings, information, and instructions.
•
Part 3 – Marshalling Violations: Listsmarshalling violations that require correction before a train 
can proceed.
o
“All Areas” messages apply to all trains.
o

6.0 Verify ing Train Area Marshalling
Supervisors in major yards and terminals are responsible for compliance with TrAM rules. 
Train crews are responsible to ensure that there are no marshalling violations applicable to the TrAM 
area(s) they will operate on. All violations must be promptly reported to a supervisor and train dispatcher.
Check the following:

Train consist:
o
Consist header messages.
o
Carinformation messages.
o
Train statistics messages.
o
Dangerous commodity messages.
o

Crew Information form for work performed enroute.

1.0 Responsib ilities of Certified Employees
Locomotive engineers, remote control operators, and conductors must:
•
Comply with all certification requirements.
•
Ensuredriving record and vision and hearing information is submitted within required timelines.
•
Know the expiration date of their certification.
•
Notify local management no less than 14 days prior to expiration of their certification.
•
Notify crew management within 48 hours of expiration of their certification.
•
Not work or accept a call to work a certified position beyond their certification expiration date.
•
Carry a current certification card or temporary certificate while on duty.
•
Present their certification card to the proper authority upon request.
•
Bequalified on the territory over which they will operate.
•
Complete a territory exam for each territory over which a qualification will be held:
o
During each recertification cycle.
o
When first qualifying over a territory.
o
Beforeoperating over a territory for which a qualification has lapsed.2.0 Motor Veh icle Driving Records
Locomotive engineers, remote control operators, and conductors must report any convictions for:
•
Operating a motor vehicle while under the influence of or impaired by a controlled substance.
•
Refusal to undergo such testing when a law enforcement official seeks to find out whether a 
person is operating under the influence of alcohol or a controlled substance.
Statesponsored diversion programs, guilty pleas, and completed state actions to cancel, revoke, 
suspend, or deny a driver’ s license are considered as applied to this rule.
An employee must report any conviction to an employee assistance representative and the Manager 
Operating Practices within 48 hours after the employee receives notice of a conviction. Managersnotified 
of a conviction by an employee must also report this information to the Operating Practices.3.0 Familiarization
Thefollowing general requirements will apply to territory familiarization:
•
Federal submissions for CF R 240 and CF R 242 will govern familiarization standards.
•
Alocomotive engineer not qualified on a specific territory will be provided a minimum of one 
round trip with a locomotive engineer pilot.
•
Aconductor not qualified on a specific territory will be provided a minimum of one round trip with 
a qualified pilot.
•
Alocomotive engineer or conductor who has not operated over a territory for a period of twelve 
consecutive months must make a minimum of one familiarization trip.

sections.text:
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
119
Glossary
Accelerometer: An instrument that displays in mph per minute the rate of speed increase or decrease.
AC Locomotive: Locomotivesequipped with AC traction motors that are not affected by short time 
ratings.
Actuate: Actionrequired to prevent an automatic brake application on the locomotive(s) or to release 
locomotive brakes from an automatic brake application.
Air Brake: Asystem of devices operated by compressed air arranged in a system and controlled 
manually, electronically, or pneumatically, that retards or arrests the motion of a car or locomotive.
Air Brake System: Acollection of devices required for the operating air brakes to control the speed of 
and stop a locomotive or train.
Air Compressor: Alocomotive device, powered by the diesel engine or an electric motor, that 
compresses air for operating the air brakes and all other air-operated devices on locomotives 
and cars.
Air Flow Indicator: An instrument that measures the air flow through the automatic brake valve to the 
brake pipe.
Air Gauge: An instrument that indicates air pressure in pounds per square inch (PSI).
Alerter: Adevice that initiates a penalty brake application when the locomotive engineer does not 
maintain the required frequency of movements of the controls.
Angle Cock: Adeviceused to open and close the brake pipe on the ends of locomotives and cars.
Articulated Car: Acarconstructed by permanently connecting two or more platforms with an articulated 
joint.
Automatic Brake Valve: Adevice that controls the flow of main reservoir air into the equalizing reservoir 
and brake pipe to charge and release brakes.
Automatic Brake Valve Cut Out Valve: Adeviceused to cut the automatic brake in or out.
“B” End: The end of a freight car where the hand brake is located, unless otherwise identified.
Bleed: Atermused to describe the venting of air to atmosphere on a car by manual operation of the 
release valve.
Block of Cars: Two or more cars coupled together that have previously received a Class Ior Class IA air 
brake test for which the Train Brake Status is available.
Block Swap: Adding a maximum of one car or solid block of cars, qualified by the required air brake test 
and safety inspection, to another through train.
Brake Application: Abrake pipe pressure reduction that causes the control valve to move to the service 
or emergency position.
CPKC | U n i t e d S t a t e s A i r B r a ke
 a n d T r a i n H a n d l i n g
119

120
CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
Brake Cylinder: Ametallic cylinder containing a piston. Compressed air forces the piston outward to 
apply the brakes. When the air pressure is released, the piston returns to its normal position by a release 
spring coiled around the piston rod inside the cylinder.
Brake Cylinder Release Valve: The valve that initially bleeds brake cylinder pressure. I f held open, it will 
bleed auxiliary and emergency reservoir pressures.
Brake Indicator: Adevice which indicates the brake application range and indicates whether brakes are 
applied and released.
Brake Pipe: The pipe, angle cocks, hoses, and hose couplings that distribute compressed air throughout 
the automatic brake system.
Brake Pipe Gradient: The difference in brake pipe pressure between the locomotive or air source and 
the rear car of the train. 
Branch Pipe Cut out Cock: Adevice on locomotives and cars that isolates the control valve from 
the brake pipe.
Brake Pipe Pressure: The amount of pressure contained in the brake pipe, commonly expressed in 
pounds per square inch (psi).
Buff Force: Compressive coupler forces that occur during a slack-bunched condition.
Communication Loss Idle Down: Adistributed power feature that detects a change in brake pipe 
pressure during an interruption of distributed power radio communication. Alsoreferred to as Comm Loss 
Idle Down. 
Continuity: The ability to transmit a brake signal between the lead locomotive and the last piece of 
equipment on the train.
Control Valve: The valve on locomotives and cars that charges reservoirs and applies or releases brake 
cylinder pressure in response to changes in brake pipe pressure.
Coupler Alignment Control: Speciallyequipped couplers, installed on most locomotives that only allow 
the coupler in buff to move laterally within certain limits.
Cut Out Cock or Valve: Adeviceused to cut in or cut out certain air brake functions.
Cycle Braking: The process of applying, releasing, and reapplying train brakes to control speed without 
completely recharging the train brake system.
DC Locomotive: Locomotivesequipped with D Ctraction motors.
Dead Engine Cut Out: Adevice near the locomotive control valve used when a locomotive unit is 
handled dead-in-train. When the dead engine cut out cock is opened, the number 2 main reservoir is 
charged from the brake pipe to operate the locomotive brakes.
Dead- in- Consist: Amethod of transporting a locomotive unit or units with the diesel engine not running 
but coupled to an operating unit.
Dead- in- Tow: Hauling locomotive(s) in a train with the brake pipe coupled and the M
Uair hoses 
uncoupled.
CPKC | U n i t e d S t a t e s A i r B r a ke
 a n d T r a i n H a n d l i n g
120

CPKC | United States Air Brake and Train Handling
121
Distributed Power: One or more locomotive consists that are remotely controlled from the lead, 
locomotive.
Draft Force: Pulling force, or tension on couplers and draft gear during a slack-stretched condition.
Draft Gear: Acushioning device that transmits draft or buff forces between the coupler and the car or 
locomotive frame.
Driving Axle: Alocomotive axle used for tractive effort.
Dynamic Brake: The system that electronically converts energy created by the momentum of a moving 
locomotive into an effective retarding brake.
Dynamic Brake Factor: Anumerical value used to convey the dynamic braking capability of 
a locomotive.
Dynamic Brake Holding Feature: Afeature of the lead controlling locomotive that allows dynamic 
braking effort when a PCS open condition exists.
Emergency Application: Areduction in brake pipe pressure at a rate sufficient to cause control valves to 
move to the emergency position.
Emergency Brake Valve: Avalveused to initiate an emergency brake application.
EOT (End of Train Device): Asystem of components that determines the rear car brake pipe pressure 
and transmits that information to the display on the head-of-train telemetry device (HOT).
Equalizing Reservoir: Asmall reference volume on locomotives used to make service brake 
applications. 
False Gradient: Aterm that describes the amount of pressure present in the rear car while the 
air brake system is still recharging. False Gradient is any pressure less than True Gradient. The 
amount of False Gradient can be determined by subtracting False Gradient from True Gradient. 
Example:
88-psi – Highest obtainable rear car pressure (True Gradient)
85-psi – current rear car pressure while recharging (False Gradient)
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3-psi = Amount of false gradient
Foreign Locomotive: Any locomotive not owned by CPKC.
Foundation Brake Gear: The levers, rods, brake beams, etc. that connect the brake cylinder piston rod 
to the brake shoes. When air pressure forces the piston out, the brake shoes are forced against the 
wheels.
Full Service Application: Aservicereduction of brake pipe pressure that equalizes the pressure 
between the brake cylinder and the auxiliary reservoir.
CPKC | U n i t e d S t a t e s A i r B r a ke
 a n d T r a i n H a n d l i n g

122

Grade: The slope of railway track. Grades are classified as follows:
•
Light Grade: any grade below 1.0 percent
•
Heavy Grade: any grade between 1.0 and 1.8 percent
•
Mountain Grade: any grade greater than 1.8 percent
•
Ascending Grade: Asection of track where elevation increases
•
Cresting Grade: A
